data.title: Marvell-Lumentum Deal Reportedly Would Carry Limited Premium
data.description:
Semiconductor and data-infrastructure business Marvell Technology Inc. (MRVL, Financials) is said to be looking at an all-stock purchase of optical-networking provider Lumentum that would not provide shareholders a substantial premium.

The new story added substance to prior signs the businesses were in advanced negotiations on an acquisition.

Shares of Lumentum declined roughly 3.9% after the report, implying that investors were counting on a higher price for the purchase.

Marvell shares also came under pressure, trading down around 8.7%.

An all-stock arrangement might decrease Marvell's immediate financial requirements, but it also would dilute current owners depending on the eventual exchange ratio.

For Marvell, Lumentum would extend its reach into optical components for high-speed networking and AI data centers, a market with growing demand for faster links between GPUs and servers.

Valuation and dilution will dictate how investors see the purchase, but the strategic reasoning may be compelling.

No final transaction value, exchange ratio or verified announcement date was disclosed by the source.

Now the next trigger will be corporations publicly announcing a deal and the premium and financing parameters.

data.title: Canada Deems Vancouver Port Expansion National Priority in Bid to Diversify Trade
data.description:
By Paul Vieira

OTTAWA--Canada declared as a national priority a proposed expansion at the country's busiest port in Vancouver, British Columbia, arguing that it is required for the country to meet its goal of doubling non-U.S. exports by 2035.

The designation also kicks off an accelerated regulatory review process, whereby officials are tasked with determining how the expansion proceeds and under what conditions, as opposed to whether it requires approval.

Officials said this puts the timing for a final investment decision from the Vancouver Fraser Port Authority by mid-2027.

The authority, which manages the Vancouver port, said the expansion project would increase container capacity by about 50%, through a new land-mass and wharf structure covering 300 acres. This additional capacity could support annual trade of 100 billion Canadian dollars (US$71.5 billion).

Officials peg the project's cost at C$5.9 billion. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has pledged up to C$10 billion in financial support for Pacific coast trade corridors.

The port authority said the Vancouver terminal currently handles more than C$1 billion in commerce daily, and more cargo than the next five largest Canadian ports combined.

The expansion, upgrade and construction of trade corridors across Canada is a priority initiative for Carney, who has argued that it is necessary to restore resilience in the economy and reduce the country's reliance on U.S. trade to drive economic growth.

According to government documents, there needs to be a "significant expansion" of Canada's port capacity to diversify trade, adding that 80% of trade with non-U.S. markets is done by sea. The prime minister has set a goal of doubling the level of non-U.S. exports by 2035.

"Continued inaction on port expansion could eventually force Canadian importers and exporters to utilize U.S. ports--a dependency that is untenable in the current geopolitical circumstances," officials said, according to documents distributed at a technical briefing. "Port expansion is thus integral to ensuring Canadian sovereignty and control over key economic linkages to the rest of the world," the officials said, according to the documents.

Officials warned that without port expansion, Canada could face sharply higher shipping costs of up to C$900 million a year due to traffic congestion and insufficient capacity.

Bank of Canada researchers warned this year that the country lacked the port capacity to executive the government's trade agenda.

The central bank's analysis indicated Canadian ports can't accommodate some of the latest ultra-large container ships being deployed. Because of this, some goods originating from China and destined for Canada and loaded onto these big vessels have to dock in Los Angeles--and those goods could be subject to U.S. tariffs.

data.title: Samsung Stocks Decline 3% With Semiconductor Profit Concentration in Focus
data.description:
Samsung Electronics (SSNLF), the South Korean chip and device maker, has an AI profit engineand a growing dependence on it. Shares closed at ?225,000, down 3.02%, on October 30. Its third-quarter results put that concentration in sharp focus: semiconductors delivered ?106.5 trillion of the group's ?107.4 trillion operating profit. That works out to roughly 99.2%, making chip earnings the overwhelming driver of group profitability.

The semiconductor division generated ?147.1 trillion in revenue, while the device-experience business posted an operating loss of ?0.8 trillion. Samsung expanded HBM4 sales during the quarter and plans to push further into high-bandwidth memory, server DRAM and solid-state storage. The opportunity looks substantial, but so does the exposure: changes in memory pricing, demand or product mix could carry considerable weight across group earnings while the device business remains unprofitable.

The GuruFocus chart adds a useful valuation check. Samsung's GF Score of 92/100 pairs strong profitability, growth, financial strength and momentum with a much weaker GF Value reading. That suggests business quality and price appeal may be telling different stories; a high overall score alone does not establish a bargain. The next earnings test is whether AI memory and enterprise storage can keep delivering while the device business rebuilds profitability.

data.description: Earnings per share growth from five of the "Magnificent 7" companies has so far lagged other names in the S&P 500 Index in the third quarter, per FactSet earnings analyst John Butters. data.title: Shareholders of Brazil's Raizen vote to back restructuring plan
data.description:
By Luciana Magalhaes and Oliver Griffin

Shareholders of Brazil's Raizen , a global sugar and ethanol producer, on Friday voted to approve the implementation of the company's out-of-court restructuring plan, three people familiar with the matter told Reuters.

The package includes a planned capital increase of between 3.5 billion to 39.8 billion reais ($642.2 million to $7.3 billion), according to a company filing published on Monday.

A spokesperson for Raizen declined to comment.

Raizen's restructuring plan, totaling some 65 billion reais in debt, is the largest in Brazilian history and followed a number of risky bets, poor harvests, and low commodity prices.

The company was initially created as a joint venture between Brazilian conglomerate Cosan and London-listed oil major Shell .

($1 = 5.45 Brazilian reais)

data.title: The Fed held interest rates steady, but these officials see more hikes coming soon
data.description:
By Greg Robb

Dallas Fed's Lorie Logan sees 'at least' 50 basis points in additional hikes

Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas President Lorie Logan said that without additional rate hikes, inflation won't get back down to the 2% target.

On Friday, the first day that Federal Reserve officials were able to speak publicly about the central bank's vote earlier this week to make no change to its interest-rate policy, two top officials said the Fed would need to hike rates in coming months in order to counter inflation pressures.

The comments show there is no settled policy at the central bank when it comes to taking publicly about the economic outlook. Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh has been pulling back on commenting on how he views past data and future economic trends.

Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan and St. Louis Fed President Roberto Musalem both said it was important for the Fed to explain to investors what officials are thinking,

In a speech at Davidson College, Logan, who voted on Wednesday to keep rates unchanged, said the Fed needs to implement "at least" two more quarter-point hikes.

"I currently estimate that the fed-funds target range is at least 50 basis points - half a percentage point - below the level that would create some modest restriction and begin to bring the inflation trend back to target," Logan told students at Davidson College.

Without at least two more quarter-point rate hikes, she added, inflation will continue to trend above the Fed's 2% target, unless unexpected shocks to the economy, like a downturn, occur.

She said the Fed could pause after these moves and reassess the economic outlook.

In September, the Fed hiked interest rates by a quarter-point to a range of 3.75-4%. It was the first hike in three years and signaled a reversal of the policy of trying to engineer a soft landing for the economy by slowly bringing down interest rates and inflation at the same time. At that meeting, 16 of 18 Fed officials penciled in another hike this year.

Many economists noted that the inflation data released after the September meeting was even hotter than before the Fed raised rates, and they argued the Fed should have hiked again this week.

But the Federal Open Market Committee voted 10-2 to make no change in rates. At his press conference, Warsh said officials wanted to wait for more data before acting. Many economists criticized Warsh for not saying more about his thoughts on the road ahead. Economists said they would instead look to officials like Logan and Musalem for a sense of what may be to come.

Logan explained that she supported the pause because raising rates gradually "can help households, businesses and market participants adapt to higher rates and reduce the risk that economic activity deteriorates more sharply than necessary."

She added: "Skipping a meeting does not change the monetary-policy destination."

In a separate speech to economists in New York, Musalem also backed a plan to keep raising interest rates.

Musalem said it was his base-case scenario that inflation will only come down if there are more rate hikes.

"I judge that additional firming of monetary policy will be necessary, and soon," Musalem said.

"Moving sooner in smaller steps while inflation expectations are anchored has a better chance of succeeding without adverse impact on the labor market or economic growth," he added.

The next meeting of the Fed's interest-rate committee is Dec. 8-9.

Richmond Fed President Tom Barkin, meanwhile, didn't specifically say whether he would back more rate hikes when he spoke this week.

But Barkin noted there could be a case for higher rates if artificial-intelligence spending continued at a strong pace.

"If we do see a continued surge in demand, that would be the kind of thing you might want to lean against," Barkin said in an interview on "The Business Briefing" on Sirius XM.

"It's also the case that if we create a more productive economy and AI is leading to much stronger growth, that's an economy that can handle higher interest rates," he said.

Barkin also supported moving slowing on tightening policy.

"I think gradual makes sense when you're not much behind the curve, where you want time to learn, both from the economic environment and the external environment," he said.

-Greg Robb

data.title: Binance Heist Serves as $6.3 Billion Wake-Up Call for Crypto Security — Analysis
data.description:
By Dean Seal

Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance by compromising a single employee's laptop, giving the crypto world an expensive wake-up call to tighten basic security protocols, according to industry experts.

The breach sent cryptocurrency prices tumbling alongside another tech selloff as traders react to what is set to be the crypto industry's biggest cyber intrusion to date. People within the industry are pointing to the simplicity of the attack as a warning sign for firms and investors alike.

"It was a failure of basic corporate security," said Wojciech Kaszycki, a strategy adviser of the Polish digital asset company BTCS S.A. "A single device should never be able to move money, and a device with that kind of access should never leave the building."

While Binance is working to mitigate the damage for customers, the heist could have wider repercussions.

If withdrawal restrictions are prolonged or traders start to have doubts about exchanges' reserves, lenders and market makers could retreat, draining liquidity across platforms, according to Bitget Wallet researcher Lacie Zhang. Capital is already moving out of risk assets, she said.

"Long-term confidence depends on restored withdrawals, independently verified reserves and transparent accountability," Zhang said.

Bitcoin was down 5% at $76,694 on Friday afternoon in the U.S.

Reality Check

Experts say the theft underscores the reality that while the blockchain is safe, the centralized infrastructure surrounding it is still vulnerable. The incident comes weeks after a $388 million security breach at rival exchange Bitget.

Bitget's chief executive, Gracy Chen, said she sympathized with Binance, knowing how difficult the initial response period is after a hack. Bitget was able to cover the financial impact of the breach with a dedicated emergency reserve, she said. "Right now, the focus should be on supporting Binance's recovery efforts and protecting its users," Chen said.

The dustup has spurred calls from Chen and others in the industry to beef up cooperation between exchanges, issuers, blockchain security firms and law enforcement to crack down on crypto cyber attacks. Brickken co-founder Ludovico Rossi said the industry should adopt standards that provide a common interface for freezing tokens and carrying out recovery transfers.

"Recovery still depends on issuers being able to intervene quickly," Rossi said.

Investors Beware

As firms adapt to the fallout, both institutional and retail investors are left scrambling to secure their own holdings and reset their expectations for exchanges and their intermediaries.

Institutional investors should be demanding independent custody, segregated assets and multi-layered transaction authorization, and will likely look to limit their exposure to a single exchange, according to Moon Pursuit Capital's Utkarsh Ahuja.

Mom-and-pop traders have more limited options for safeguards, Ahuja said. But the hack should advance the conversation around safer custody solutions for all traders, he said.

As crypto emerges from the hack, the platforms that will succeed in the industry's next growth phase will have to demonstrate robust security, transparency and independently verifiable safeguards, rather than just liquidity and execution, according to Ahuja.

"Trust can no longer be assumed," Ahuja said. "It has to be earned."

data.title: Gates Industrial Shares Fall on Lower-than-Expected 3Q Revenue
data.description:
By Natalie Weger

Shares of Gates Industrial fell after the company posted lower-than-expected revenue in the third quarter.

Shares fell 10% to $23.52 on Friday. The stock is up 9% year to date.

The manufacturer of specialized industrial belts, hydraulics and fluid transfer systems logged $903.6 million in revenue, compared with $855.7 million last year. Wall Street analysts expected $904.8 million.

Gates Industrial posted a third-quarter profit of $86.5 million, or 34 cents, compared with $81.6 million, or 32 cents, the year before.

On an adjusted basis, per-share earnings were 47 cents. Analysts polled by FactSet expected 44 cents.

Gates Industrial raised its full-year adjusted per-share earnings guidance to between $1.66 and $1.72 from its previous guidance of $1.62 and $1.70. Analysts polled by FactSet expect $1.68.

The company narrowed its full-year core sales growth outlook to between 3.2% and 3.8%, compared with 2.5% to 4.5%.

data.title: Weil Gotshal's Demise Created a Surprise NYC Office Windfall — WSJ
data.description:
By Peter Grant

The collapse of Weil, Gotshal & Manges creates an unexpected prize for either the law firm or its landlord — a big chunk of prime office space on Fifth Avenue with sweeping views of Central Park.

Weil occupies about 10 floors, or nearly 450,000 square feet, at the General Motors Building in Midtown Manhattan. It pays about $121 a square foot under a lease renewal signed in 2014 that runs through 2034, according to credit rating firm KBRA.

Office tenants would likely pay more than $200 a square foot today for the firm's space that boasts some of the building's best views, according to brokers.

"There is a complete vacuum of trophy space in Midtown and this is the best tower floor block in a trophy asset," said Josh Kuriloff, executive vice chairman of Cushman & Wakefield.

For now, it is unclear whether that windfall will go to Weil or the building's owner, a venture led by real-estate giant BXP.

If the law firm seeks bankruptcy protection, it could ask for court approval to sell its below-market lease to another tenant. But BXP could argue that a replacement tenant can't meet the lease's obligations.

Another possibility would be for BXP to pay Weil to surrender the lease as the firm dissolves, freeing the landlord to rent the space at the current higher rates.

BXP also has to refinance its 3.43% mortgage next year, which could give Weil some leverage in negotiations. The landlord has an incentive to resolve the issue before approaching lenders, who will want to know how much rent they can count on to cover the new loan.

The landlord would certainly relish getting the lease back, office brokers say. BXP President Doug Linde said on an earnings call this week that there was a "vast gap" between existing rents at the GM Building and current market rents.

The GM tower was designed by Emery Roth & Sons and completed 58 years ago at the southeast corner of Central Park, across from the famed Plaza Hotel.

The 50-story tower opened as a showcase for American corporate might, housing General Motors' New York headquarters and a ground-floor showroom displaying the automaker's latest models. Weil moved in that same year, beginning a tenancy that has lasted nearly six decades.

In 1998, Donald Trump teamed with insurer Conseco to buy the tower for $878 million. Trump also managed the property and emblazoned his name in four-foot-high gold letters on its white-marble facade.

The partnership unraveled into a bitter struggle for control, ending in 2003 when Conseco won a ruling forcing Trump to sell his stake. The gold letters pried from the building became collectors' items, turning up in offices around the city.

The building continued to make headlines after developer Harry Macklowe bought it for $1.4 billion in 2003. He brought in Apple, whose underground store opened in 2006 beneath a striking glass cube and became one of Fifth Avenue's biggest retail draws.

In 2008, amid mounting debt troubles, Macklowe sold the tower to a BXP-led venture for $2.8 billion — twice what he had paid and then a record for a U.S. office building.

Today, the GM Building is benefiting from Manhattan's emergence as the country's strongest office market.

Coco's at Colette, a members-only restaurant perched on the 37th floor, has emerged as New York City's new power lunch spot. Toy store FAO Schwarz attracted generations of tourists and children there for decades, in a space now occupied by luxury brand Moncler's global flagship store.

While much of the U.S. has suffered high vacancy following the pandemic, New York's leading law firms and financial companies are paying up for prime locations, sweeping views and lavish amenities.

Manhattan's office availability rate fell to 13.4% in the third quarter and was approaching single digits for the highest-quality space, according to Avison Young.

"The fight for talent and the fight for retention is playing out in real estate," said Rory Murphy, head of Avison Young's New York office.

With options shrinking, interest is already growing in Weil's top shelf offices high above Central Park. "I think every broker in this market is tracking the GM Building," Murphy said.

data.title: Grains Futures End Month With a Whimper — Daily Grain Highlights
data.description:
By Anthony Harrup

  • Corn for December delivery fell 0.8% Friday on the Chicago Board of Trade to $4.47 3/4 a bushel, trading around the $4.50 level as the market continues to look for more demand signals.
  • Soybeans for January delivery settled little changed at $12.34 1/4 a bushel.
  • Wheat for December delivery ended near flat at $6.03 1/4 a bushel.

The Right Price: Grains traders are focused on finding a price level that will stimulate demand and help rally the markets, said Brian Hoops of Midwest Market Solutions.

Wheat in particular tried to rally on news that China had inquired about U.S. wheat, "but an inquiry and a purchase are different things and no purchases have been announced," he said. If China does buy wheat, it should lift both wheat and corn "as it would be an indication that demand will improve at current price levels."

Flash Sales: The USDA reported two new flash sales of soybeans for the 2026-27 marketing year, one for 165,150 metric tons and another for 132,000 tons, both to unknown destinations.

Soybean export sales have had a strong start to the 2026-27 marketing year, but "strong harvest reports and a good start to the South American growing season have kept managed funds in liquidation mode," Doug Bergman of RCM Alternatives said in a note.

INSIGHT

Rain Delay: The soybean and corn harvests could be interrupted as more rain is expected this weekend and early next week across much of the Midwest, Mike Castle of StoneX said in a note.

Systems are already moving across much of Texas/Oklahoma and northern Missouri into Iowa/Illinois, "likely knocking combines back out of the field and slowing the tail-end of harvest," he said. "It will be interesting to keep an eye on the impact seen in the cash markets given the combination of delayed harvest and sharply lower prices reducing farmers' incentive to sell across the scale."

Weather Watch: It is difficult to be bearish corn under $4.50 a bushel, wheat under $6 and soybeans under $12.30 unless favorable Brazilian weather is confirmed in November-December, AgResource said in a note. Brazilian forecasts will be in focus starting next week, and while there are no problems with Argentine soil moisture or pace of corn and soy planting, there is a significant risk of a lingering El Niño negatively affecting rainfall in key soybean producing regions of Brazil, the firm added.

AHEAD

  • The USDA is scheduled to release its weekly Grain Export Inspections Report at 11 a.m. EST Monday.
  • The USDA is due to release its monthly Grain Crushings Report at 3 p.m. EST Monday.
  • The USDA is scheduled to release its monthly Oilseed Crushings Report at 3 p.m. EST Monday.
  • The USDA is due to release its weekly Crop Progress Report at 4 p.m. EST Monday.
  • Archer-Daniels Midland Co. is scheduled to announce its 3Q earnings before the stock market opens Tuesday.

data.title: Caregivers are now spending more than $11,000 a year out of pocket-up 60% in five years
data.description:
By Beth Pinsker

AARP study shows the financial sacrifices families make-and their long-term impacts

You may feel like you're just helping out a little, but before long, the average caregiver spends more than $11,000 a year.

Financial caregiving often starts slow. Mom has a big doctor's appointment, so you fly in. Everyone is so exhausted after that you spring for takeout. Maybe you notice groceries are low, so you make a delivery order. Before you know it, you're deep in it.

How deep? The new average out-of-pocket cost is a staggering $11,508, according to a major study from AARP.

"When you're in the act of caregiving, you're thinking about the actual tasks. You're not thinking about what you are pulling out of your pocket," said Rita Choula, senior director of caregiving at the AARP Public Policy Institute. "If I'm taking my mom to the doctor, I'm not thinking about the gas or the copay I pick up."

The small things add up. The average caregiver gives over 31% of their budget to caregiving costs, putting them at financial risk. The AARP survey found that 75% of caregivers had taken an adverse financial action to cover costs. Nearly 50% dipped into retirement savings and 38% limited their retirement savings. Half took a private loan and more than a third cut personal spending or dipped into their personal savings.

These are not exaggerated or unscientific guesses, but rather the result of years of caregiver research by AARP. The organization updates its out-of-pocket cost averages every five years. The last was in 2021, when the average spend was $7,242. The dollar figures come from AARP asking survey respondents to document actual spending on caregiving for a week.

The study attributed the massive increase to rising healthcare costs and increased caregiver responsibilities, along with easier access to digital solutions that allow family and friends to arrange care from afar, like paying bills and ordering online.

Choula said it was eye-opening for the participants. "The individuals providing care just don't think about it. They don't realize when they aren't able to save any more, or their bank account is lower. When they really took the time and were really intentional about it, they could see how rapidly these dollars add up."

What financial caregivers do

Many people who write a check here or there or help with tax returns don't consider themselves caregivers, which they said meant handling hands-on medical tasks. But AARP found a wide range in the tasks that people do as financial caregivers and what they pay for.

Most of the money goes toward household needs: groceries, bills and housing costs. A third went toward medical expenses like copays and equipment, and 11% went toward personal costs for the caregiver, such as travel and babysitters to cover child care.

The type of illness involved and the living situation drove differences in caregiving costs. For spouse caregivers living with the care recipients, costs were much lower than for an adult child caring for an aging parent but not living with them. African-American and Asian caregivers faced much higher costs than white ones. Care for an ill person under 40 was particularly high - $4,700 more per year than the out-of-pocket average.

A recent study on financial caregiving by financial firm Edward Jones broke down tasks of a financial caregiver in more detail, tallying it at an average of 109 hours per month. Almost three-fourths assisted the care recipient in paying bills, and nearly 70% helped them manage their bank accounts. More than half also managed health services, protected them from fraud and handled investing. Only 29% offered support managing real estate.

"Caregiving deserves as much attention as the other areas of our personal lives that we plan for," said Meilii Gensler, a managing director at Edward Jones. "The biggest thing to do is start the conversation before care is needed. Don't put yourself or anyone else you love in a more difficult position."

Long-term effects

Planning helps. When a family is in emergency mode, they may not see the risk to their finances in some of these actions, particularly the dip in retirement contributions or the impact of early withdrawals.

"The numbers are staggering and the long-term implications are great," said Angela Antonelli, a research professor and the executive director of the Center for Retirement Initiatives at Georgetown University's McCourt School of Public Policy. "The younger caregiver population is stepping into roles that could last 10 to 15 years, and the damage is unrecoverable. It's mind-blowing."

The Edward Jones study calculated the average caregiving spend at $8,737, but it was focused on caregiving for older adults, while the AARP study included caregiving for disabled younger people. The study also found that when the care recipient didn't have enough funds of their own, the average caregiver net contribution rose to $12,863 a year. When the care recipient had been the subject of financial fraud, the caregiver net contributions averaged $10,583 a year. Some 70% reported making a financial sacrifice to provide care.

Nearly 20% of the more than 3,000 caregivers surveyed stopped work entirely to focus on caregiving, while 24% took unpaid leave and 22% passed up a promotion or other career opportunity. Some 7% had to declare bankruptcy.

Edward Jones

"What struck me the most is the breadth of it - there are 33 million people providing financial caregiving in the U.S. That's not a niche population," said Gensler. "They are spending about 3.5 hours a day doing this. That's a part-time job; that's a huge time commitment."

Both AARP and Edward Jones offered possible solutions to the financial impact on caregivers, mostly involving more financial support for the care recipient and more resources and training for the caregivers.

AARP outlined a five-point plan for change in its report that starts with the government allowing caregivers to use their own pretax health accounts (FSAs or HSAs) for caregiving costs, including increased tax credits for caregivers and compensation for care work.

A key part of this is expanding training for caregivers, both on the medical side and financial side. "Many people think Medicare pays for long-term care," said Choula, "So right from the start there's some financial literacy that needs to occur."

data.title: Ten-Year Treasury Yield Slumps To Lowest Level In Well Over A Month
data.description:
WASHINGTON (dpa-AFX) - Treasuries showed a strong move to the upside during trading on Friday, extending the notable advance seen in the previous session.

Bond prices jumped early in the session and remained firmly positive throughout the day. As a result, the yield on the benchmark ten-year note, which moves opposite of its price, slumped 6.0 basis points to 4.929 percent.

The ten-year yield added to the 5.6 basis points drop seen during Thursday's session, falling to its lowest level in well over a month.

Treasuries benefitted from their appeal as a safe haven amid the substantial weakness on Wall Street, with technology stocks leading the sell-off.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq has plunged by 3.5 percent to its lowest levels in three months amid renewed concerns about the artificial intelligence trade.

Intel (INTC) has helped lead the tech sector lower, with the semiconductor giant plummeting by 31 percent to a six-month intraday low.

The nosedive by Intel comes after the company reported better than expected third quarter earnings but provided disappointing fourth quarter guidance.

Meanwhile, bond traders seemed to shrug off the inflation worries raised by a renewed surge in the price of crude oil.

U.S. crude oil futures have jumped by more than 2 percent on the day amid concerns about supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

data.title: AMZN Stock Set To Drop For Third Straight Week: Amazon Taps $80B Credit Line To Fund AI Capex
data.description:
Key points:
  • Amazon secured access to up to $80 billion in discretionary borrowing through supplier financing agreements running from early 2027 through Q3 2028. 
  • Heavy investments in data centers and equipment led to a $42.4 billion free cash outflow for the year ended Sept. 30.
  • Leaving behind its traditional cash-and-bonds approach, Amazon is embracing flexible collateralized financing alongside competitors to purchase costly hardware like Nvidia AI chips. 

Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN) has arranged up to $80 billion in supplier financing credit line as it prepares for aggressive infrastructure spending to power its artificial intelligence initiatives.

The new credit structure gives the e-commerce and cloud provider additional financial flexibility while committing hundreds of billions toward data center construction and advanced hardware.

AMZN stock eased about 2% on Friday and is set to end its third consecutive week lower.

New Way Of Funding

According to a quarterly regulatory filing disclosed Thursday, the secured credit line allows Amazon to borrow against the value of purchased hardware at its own discretion.

The facility opens at the start of 2027 and runs through the third quarter of 2028. Lenders participating in the agreement will hold collateral rights over specific assets acquired via the facility. Amazon has not detailed which specific equipment will serve as collateral, and representatives for the company declined to provide further specifics.

Speaking on Bloomberg Television on Friday, Matt Garman, Chief Executive Officer of Amazon Web Services, highlighted the rationale behind the strategy. "When we see such a really large opportunity in front of us, we're looking for ways to also responsibly fund that so that we can go as big as possible for our customers," Garman said. He added that the firm is collaborating with key partners to better balance operational cash flows during this rapid operational buildup.

Shift From Traditional Funding

Historically, Amazon financed its cloud computing infrastructure and semiconductor acquisitions directly from retail and cloud revenue streams or through corporate bond issuances.

The company previously refrained from complex financing arrangements, such as joint venture construction deals or third-party chip leases. Such structures have become commonplace among competing technology companies seeking to acquire expensive Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) processors, which represent a significant portion of modern data center expenditures.

Capital Outlays Drive Cash Outflows

The move comes after Amazon reported higher-than-anticipated third-quarter capital expenditures. The increased spending contributed to a free cash outflow of $42.4 billion for the 12 months ending Sept. 30.

The company's aggregate future financial commitments, which include outstanding debt, interest payments, uncommenced leases, and equipment purchase obligations, reached $883 billion at the end of September, a 36% jump from the prior quarter.

Retail sentiment on Stocktwits was ‘bullish’ with ‘high’ message volumes.

AMZN stock has gained about 3% year-to-date.
